questions.stem: On a Mercator chart, which line is drawn straight?
options: A rhumb line, meaning a line of constant course
A great circle between two distant ports
The shortest path between two places on the globe
A line of constant magnetic variation
questions.explanation: A Mercator chart is built so that a line cutting every meridian at the same angle (a rhumb line, i.e. a steady course) is straight. The great circle and the shortest path are the same thing and are straight on a gnomonic chart, not on Mercator. Lines of equal variation are curves on any chart.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say a Mercator chart is conformal?
options: Distances are the same everywhere on the chart
Areas of land and water are shown in true proportion
Great circles appear as straight lines
Angles and the shapes of small areas are shown correctly, so a direction measured on the chart is the true direction
questions.explanation: Conformal means angle-true. That is why a course laid with parallel rules reads correctly on the compass rose. It does not mean distances are constant (the latitude scale grows poleward), it does not preserve area (high latitudes look enlarged), and straight great circles belong to the gnomonic projection.

questions.stem: Why can the poles not be shown on a Mercator chart?
options: The meridians never meet on a Mercator chart, so the chart has no north edge
The chart datum is undefined north of 80 degrees
The parallels are spaced further and further apart toward the poles, and the spacing grows without limit as latitude approaches 90 degrees
The compass rose cannot be drawn there
questions.explanation: To keep angles true while the meridians are drawn parallel, the spacing of the parallels is stretched by the same ratio as the meridians were stretched. That ratio grows without limit near the pole, so the pole sits infinitely far away. The other options invent reasons that have nothing to do with the projection.

questions.stem: A navigator draws a great-circle track on a gnomonic chart. What is the normal next step?
options: Read the course directly from the compass rose on the gnomonic chart
Use the gnomonic chart's single distance scale to measure the whole track
Steer the track as drawn, because gnomonic charts are working charts
Pick points along the line and transfer them to a Mercator chart, joining them with rhumb-line legs
questions.explanation: A gnomonic chart shows great circles as straight lines but is neither conformal nor equal-area, so courses and distances cannot be measured on it. The points are carried to a Mercator chart where courses are laid and steered in short rhumb-line legs.

questions.stem: Which of these charts shows the most detail of a small harbour?
options: A 1:10 000 harbour plan
A 1:80 000 approach chart
A 1:350 000 coastal chart
A 1:3 500 000 passage chart
questions.explanation: The chart with the smallest second number is the largest scale. A large-scale chart shows a small area in great detail. The others cover progressively more area with less detail, so each is a smaller scale than the one before.

questions.stem: On a chart of scale 1:25 000 you measure 9.26 cm between two points. What is the ground distance?
options: 2.3 nm
0.8 nm
questions.explanation: 9.26 cm x 25 000 = 231 500 cm = 2315 m. Dividing by 1852 m per nautical mile gives 1.25 nm. 2.3 comes from stopping at kilometres and calling them miles, 0.8 comes from dividing by 25 000 twice over, and 12.5 is a decimal slip.

questions.stem: On a chart of scale 1:75 000, about how long on the chart is a passage of 3 nm?
options: 4.0 cm
7.4 cm
questions.explanation: 3 nm = 3 x 1852 = 5556 m = 555 600 cm. Dividing by 75 000 gives 7.4 cm. 4.0 cm uses 1000 m for a mile, 0.74 cm drops a decimal place, and 11.1 cm would be a 4.5 nm passage.

questions.stem: A leg lies near 50 degrees N on a Mercator chart that spans 48 to 53 degrees N. Which scale do you use to measure its length?
options: The part of the latitude scale at the side of the chart, level with the leg
The longitude scale along the bottom edge
The representative fraction in the title block, because it is exact at every latitude
A part of the latitude scale far from the leg, because every minute is the same length
questions.explanation: On a Mercator chart the length of a minute of latitude changes with latitude, so you read distance on the side scale level with the work. The longitude scale is wrong because a minute of longitude is shorter than a mile away from the equator. The title-block fraction is stated for one latitude only.

questions.stem: Which statement matches Navigation Safety Regulations, 2020, s. 142 for charts?
options: Any charts of the area may be used, preferably the smallest scale that covers the whole voyage
The most recent versions of the applicable charts in their largest scale for each area to be navigated must be kept on board, with the reference catalogue and the annual Notices to Mariners
Charts printed within the last five years are acceptable without corrections
Only the charts for the first leg of the voyage must be on board before departure
questions.explanation: Section 142(1)(a) and (b) ask for the reference catalogue, the applicable charts in their largest scale, and the annual edition of Notices to Mariners, in respect of each area where the vessel is scheduled to be navigated. The regulation says nothing about a five-year age limit, and the smallest scale is the opposite of the requirement.

questions.stem: Before a chart is used to plan and execute a voyage, what does s. 146 require?
options: It must carry a printing date within the current year
It must have been approved by a chart agent in the port of departure
It must be compared with the track of the previous voyage
It must be correct and up to date from Notices to Mariners or a navigational warning
questions.explanation: Section 146(1) puts the duty on the master to make sure charts, documents and publications are corrected from Notices to Mariners or navigational warnings. A recent edition date alone is not enough, because corrections issued after printing are your responsibility.

questions.stem: A 60 GT Canadian vessel works the same stretch of coast every week. Her master knows the charted routes, lights, buoys, hazards, tides, currents and weather patterns of the area well. How does s. 142(1) apply to her?
options: It applies in full, because the only exception is for vessels of 8 m or less
It does not apply if the person in charge of navigation has sufficient knowledge of the area that safety and efficiency of navigation are not compromised
It does not apply, because every vessel under 100 gross tonnage is exempt automatically
It applies to the charts but not to the Sailing Directions and tide tables
questions.explanation: Section 142(3) removes the requirement for a vessel under 100 gross tonnage only when the person in charge of navigation has sufficient knowledge of the charted routes, lights, buoys and marks, hazards and the prevailing conditions. The exemption is a knowledge test, not an automatic tonnage exemption, and it covers the whole of subsection (1), not just the charts.
